name: Apache DataFusion
summary: A query engine library in Rust, built on Arrow, that other projects embed and extend to build their own databases and data tools.
intro: DataFusion is a query engine you compile into your own program, not a server you connect to. You hand it SQL or build a query with its DataFrame API. It parses and plans the query, rewrites the plan with its optimiser, then runs it on a streaming, multi-threaded, vectorised engine that passes Apache Arrow record batches between operators. It keeps no storage of its own: it reads Parquet, CSV, JSON and Avro files from local disk or object storage such as S3, in-memory Arrow data, or any source you plug in, and writes results back with `COPY ... TO` or `INSERT INTO`.

Almost every layer can be replaced: table sources (the `TableProvider` trait), scalar, aggregate and window functions, optimiser rules, and logical and physical plan nodes. That makes it a kit for building data systems, and dozens do: InfluxDB 3, the Arroyo stream processor, delta-rs, Lance, GreptimeDB, Spice.ai, Cloudflare’s R2 query engine and the dbt Fusion engine among them. Subprojects add a command-line client (`datafusion-cli`), Python bindings (`pip install datafusion`), Ballista for running queries across several machines, and Comet, a plugin that runs Apache Spark jobs on DataFusion. A new major version ships every two to three months; the current one is 55.1.0.
strengths: A full SQL planner, optimiser and vectorised engine you can embed instead of writing your own
Extension points at every layer: data sources, functions, optimiser rules and execution operators
Works on Arrow, so results pass to other Arrow tools in Python, Rust and elsewhere without conversion
Apache 2.0 licensed and governed by the ASF, with many companies building on and contributing to it
Reads Parquet efficiently from object storage, skipping row groups and pages that can’t match
limits: It’s a library, not a database: no server, user management or persistent catalog unless you build them or use a product built on it
Customising it means writing Rust; the extension APIs are Rust traits
Each major release can break the Rust API, and majors arrive every few months, so embedders must budget for upgrades
One process by default; running across machines needs Ballista or a distributed layer of your own

items.name: DataFusion
items.text: The core: SQL and DataFrame APIs, planner, optimiser and execution engine, added to a Rust project as a dependency.

items.name: datafusion-cli
items.text: An interactive SQL shell. Queries files by path, including `s3://` and `gs://` locations, or as external tables.

items.name: DataFusion Python
items.text: Python bindings with SQL and a lazy DataFrame API. Reads pandas, Polars and Arrow data, and returns results in any of them.

items.name: Ballista
items.text: A scheduler and executors that spread DataFusion queries across many machines. Andy Grove donated it to Apache Arrow in 2021.

items.name: Comet
items.text: Translates Spark physical plans into DataFusion plans and runs them natively, with no code changes. Started at Apple, donated in 2024, 1.0 in August 2026.

sections.title: DataFusion or DuckDB?
sections.intro: Both are fast, embeddable, columnar SQL engines that run on one machine. They are aimed at different people.

story: Apache Spark ran on the JVM, and much of its engineering went into working around that: Java serialization between nodes, garbage collection and out-of-memory errors that took constant tuning. Andy Grove noted that Spark’s Project Tungsten was, in effect, “making a JVM product make less use of the JVM”. In 2017 he started DataFusion to test a hypothesis: a Spark-like engine written in Rust would be fast even when naive, and more predictable and reliable.

After rebuilding it on Arrow’s Rust library, Grove donated DataFusion to the Apache Arrow project in February 2019. It could then run simple SQL over CSV files. In 2021 he donated Ballista, a distributed engine built on it. Companies that needed a query engine began building on DataFusion instead of writing one: InfluxData chose it for InfluxDB 3.0 rather than spend what its engineers estimated at tens of person-years building another engine, and Apple donated Comet, its Spark accelerator, in 2024.
In April 2024 DataFusion left Arrow to become a top-level Apache project, as more contributors worked on it alone rather than alongside the Arrow Rust library.

choices.why: Grove saw Spark’s performance and reliability problems as coming from Java serialization and garbage collection. Rust gives native speed and predictable memory use without a garbage collector.
The 2019 rewrite made DataFusion Arrow-native, so data passes between DataFusion, Arrow libraries and other Arrow-based engines without copying or conversion.

choices.choice: A library with extension points everywhere
choices.why: A complete engine takes tens of person-years. Making sources, functions, optimiser rules and operators replaceable lets projects such as InfluxDB reuse that work and add only what is specific to them.
